questions.question: A ball is thrown at 9.70 m s-1 at 49.0 degrees to the horizontal towards a wall 5.00 m away. Show that the ball reaches the wall in about 0.8 s.
questions.answer: Horizontal velocity 9.70 cos 49.0 = 6.36 m s-1, so t = 5.00 / 6.36 = 0.79 s (about 0.8 s).
steps: Resolve the velocity horizontally: u_x = 9.70 cos 49.0 = 6.36 m s-1.
Horizontal motion has no acceleration (air resistance ignored), so distance = u_x t.
t = 5.00 / 6.36 = 0.786 s, which rounds to 0.8 s.

questions.question: The top of the wall is 3.00 m above the release point. Deduce whether the ball in part (a) (initial speed 9.70 m s-1 at 49.0 degrees) goes over the wall.
questions.answer: No. At the wall (t = 0.786 s) the ball is about 2.72 m above the release point, below the 3.00 m top, so it hits the wall.
steps: Vertical component: u_y = 9.70 sin 49.0 = 7.32 m s-1.
Time to reach the wall t = 0.786 s from part (a).
2.72 m is less than 3.00 m, so the ball is below the top of the wall when it reaches it and does not go over.

questions.question: An object accelerates from rest down a frictionless slope at 23 degrees to the horizontal, moving a distance of 20 m. Which expression gives its final speed? The options A to D are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: C: sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 20 x sin 23)  (about 12 m s^-1)
steps: The slope is frictionless, so the only force along it is the component of weight, mg sin 23, giving acceleration a = g sin 23 down the slope.
The object starts from rest (u = 0) and moves s = 20 m along the slope, so v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 2 x (9.81 sin 23) x 20.
v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 20 x sin 23) = 12.4 m s^-1, which is option C.
Options A and B use cos 23 (the wrong component), and B and D use 0.5 instead of 2, so they are wrong.

questions.question: A golf ball is hit at 33 m s-1 at 28 degrees to the horizontal. From the lower level it lands 92 m away. A higher level 4.5 m above the lower level is meant to add 10 m. Deduce whether the higher level is sufficient, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: No. From the higher level the ball travels about 99.8 m horizontally to the lower level, an increase of about 7.8 m, which is less than 10 m.
steps: Components: u_x = 33 cos 28 = 29.1 m s-1 and u_y = 33 sin 28 = 15.5 m s-1.
Check the lower level: R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g = 33^2 sin 56 / 9.81 = 92.0 m, which agrees with the given value.
From the higher level the ball lands 4.5 m lower: -4.5 = 15.5t - 4.905t^2 gives t = 3.43 s (positive root).
Horizontal distance x = u_x t = 29.1 x 3.43 = 99.8 m.
Increase = 99.8 - 92.0 = 7.8 m, which is less than the 10 m required, so the upper level is not sufficient.

questions.question: The trajectories of the golf ball with and without air resistance are shown. Explain the differences between the two paths.
questions.answer: With air resistance the ball has a shorter range, a lower maximum height and a steeper, asymmetric descent, because drag opposes the motion and removes energy.
steps: Without air resistance the only force is weight: the horizontal velocity is constant, the vertical acceleration is g, and the path is a symmetric parabola (dashed).
With air resistance, a drag force acts opposite to the velocity, so the horizontal velocity decreases continuously; the ball covers less horizontal distance, giving a shorter range.

On the way up, drag has a downward component as well as weight, so the deceleration is greater than g; the vertical velocity falls to zero sooner, giving a lower maximum height and a shorter time to the top.
The horizontal velocity is lower on the way down, so the path is steeper than on the way up: the curve is not symmetric and the peak is nearer the launch point.
Drag increases with speed, so the effect is greatest near the start (high speed), and the ball loses kinetic energy as work is done against drag (transferred as heat to the air).
The ball therefore lands at a lower speed and at a steeper angle than in the no-drag case.

questions.question: A ball falls through a vertical height of 0.60 m before bouncing at point A on a ramp. Show that its velocity just before the bounce is about 3 m s-1.
questions.answer: v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.60) = 3.4 m s-1, which is about 3 m s-1 to 1 s.f.
steps: The ball is dropped from rest, so u = 0 and the acceleration is g.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as with a = g and s = 0.60 m.
v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.60) = sqrt(11.77) = 3.43 m s-1, which is about 3 m s-1 to 1 s.f.

questions.question: Kinetic energy is conserved as the ball bounces off the ramp, and the ball leaves at 70 degrees to the vertical. State expressions for the horizontal and vertical components of velocity immediately after the bounce.
questions.answer: Speed v = 3.43 m s-1 (unchanged). Horizontal component = v sin 70 (about 3.2 m s-1); vertical component = v cos 70 (about 1.2 m s-1).
steps: Kinetic energy is conserved, so the speed after the bounce equals the speed before, v = 3.43 m s-1.
The angle is measured from the vertical, so the vertical component is v cos 70 and the horizontal component is v sin 70.
Numerically: horizontal = 3.43 sin 70 = 3.2 m s-1; vertical = 3.43 cos 70 = 1.2 m s-1.

questions.question: Point A is 0.86 m vertically above the ground and 1.23 m horizontally from the end of the ramp. Deduce whether the ball will bounce a second time on the ramp.
questions.answer: No. The ball clears the end of the ramp (it is still 0.59 m above the ramp when it passes the end), so it does not bounce a second time on the ramp.
steps: After the bounce, speed v = sqrt(2gh) = 3.43 m s^-1 at 70 degrees to the vertical, so horizontal velocity = 3.43 sin 70 = 3.22 m s^-1 and vertical velocity = 3.43 cos 70 = 1.17 m s^-1 upwards.
Time to travel the 1.23 m horizontal length of the ramp: t = 1.23 / 3.22 = 0.381 s.
Vertical displacement from A in this time: s = ut + 1/2 at^2 = 1.17 x 0.381 - 0.5 x 9.81 x 0.381^2 = -0.27 m (0.27 m below A).
The ramp end is 0.86 m below A, so the ball is about 0.59 m above the ramp end when it reaches it, and has not hit the ramp.

Check: the ball reaches the ground after 0.555 s, at 1.79 m from A, beyond the 1.23 m end of the ramp, so it lands on the ground. The ramp slopes down at tan^-1(0.86/1.23) = 35 degrees, while the ball leaves at only 20 degrees above the horizontal, so it moves away from the ramp surface.

questions.question: A firework is designed to explode at a maximum height of 350 m. Show that the vertical component of its velocity at launch is about 80 m s-1.
questions.answer: v_y = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 350) = 82.9 m s-1, which is about 80 m s-1 to 1 s.f.
steps: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as with v = 0, a = -g and s = 350 m, so u_y^2 = 2gh.
u_y = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 350) = sqrt(6867) = 82.9 m s-1, which rounds to about 80 m s-1.

questions.question: The vertical component of launch velocity depends on the initial velocity and the angle theta to the horizontal. Sketch a graph of the initial velocity needed to reach the 350 m maximum height against the angle theta.
questions.answer: u = 82.9 / sin theta: a curve falling steeply at small angles, reaching a minimum of 83 m s-1 at 90 degrees (u is about 166 m s-1 at 30 degrees).
steps: The vertical component is fixed at u_y = 82.9 m s-1 by the 350 m height.
u sin theta = 82.9, so u = 82.9 / sin theta.
Sketch: u is very large for small theta, falls as theta increases, and is smallest (82.9 m s-1) when theta = 90 degrees.
Check points: theta = 30 gives 166 m s-1; theta = 60 gives 96 m s-1.

questions.question: A student estimates the time between seeing the firework explode and hearing it, and the angle from the top to the bottom of the firework. Describe how the maximum diameter can be determined from these estimates.
questions.answer: Distance d = (speed of sound) x (time delay); diameter D = 2d tan(theta/2), where theta is the angle subtended at the observer.
steps: Light arrives almost instantly, so the time delay is the time for sound to travel the distance.
Distance d = v_sound x t, using the speed of sound in air (about 340 m s-1).
The firework subtends angle theta at the observer, so its diameter is D = 2 d tan(theta / 2).
This gives the maximum diameter from the estimated data.

questions.question: A skier moving at 25 m s-1 leaves a ramp angled upwards at 10 degrees to the horizontal. A flat surface starts 30 m horizontally from the ramp and is 2.9 m below the ramp. Deduce whether the skier reaches the flat surface before landing, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: Yes. The skier lands about 32.7 m horizontally from the ramp, beyond the 30 m edge, so lands on the flat surface.
steps: Components: u_x = 25 cos 10 = 24.6 m s-1 and u_y = 25 sin 10 = 4.34 m s-1 (upwards).
Landing 2.9 m below the ramp: -2.9 = 4.34t - 4.905t^2, giving t = 1.33 s.
Horizontal distance at landing: x = 24.6 x 1.33 = 32.7 m.
At x = 30 m, t = 1.22 s and the height is 2.0 m below the ramp, i.e. 0.9 m above the flat surface, so the skier is still in the air over the surface.
Since 32.7 m is greater than 30 m, the skier lands on the flat surface.

questions.question: A second skier of mass 63 kg travels along a horizontal surface at 23 m s-1 and comes to rest after 43 m. Calculate the average force needed to bring the skier to rest.
questions.answer: Average force about 390 N (387 N), opposing the motion.
steps: Newton's second law: F = ma = 63 x 6.15 = 388 N.
The force acts opposite to the motion, and rounds to about 390 N.

questions.question: A rugby ball is kicked off the ground at 35.0 degrees to the horizontal and reaches a maximum height of 5.0 m. Show that its initial speed is about 17 m s-1.
steps: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gh with v_y = 0.
u = u_y / sin 35.0 = 9.90 / 0.574 = 17.3 m s-1, which is about 17 m s-1.

questions.question: After a horizontal distance of 22.0 m the ball reaches the goal. The ball must be more than 3.00 m above the ground to score. Deduce whether an initial speed of 17.0 m s-1 at 35.0 degrees is sufficient to score.
questions.answer: Yes, marginally. At 22.0 m the ball is about 3.16 m above the ground, which is more than 3.00 m.
steps: Components with u = 17.0: u_x = 17.0 cos 35.0 = 13.9 m s-1 and u_y = 17.0 sin 35.0 = 9.75 m s-1.
Time to reach the goal: t = 22.0 / 13.9 = 1.58 s.
3.16 m is greater than 3.00 m, so the ball is high enough to score.

questions.question: An explosion projects a rock at 50 m s-1 at 40 degrees to the horizontal. Show that the rock reaches its maximum height about 3 s after the explosion.
questions.answer: t = u sin 40 / g = 50 sin 40 / 9.81 = 3.28 s, which is about 3 s to 1 s.f.
steps: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero.
Use v = u + at with v = 0 and a = -g: t = u_y / g.

questions.question: The rock moves in the direction of a hill whose side is at 20 degrees to the horizontal, and lands on the side of the hill. Deduce whether the rock hits the hillside before it reaches its maximum height.
questions.answer: No. The rock reaches its maximum height at 3.3 s and only meets the hillside at 3.7 s, so it does not hit the ground before it reaches its maximum height.
steps: Components: u_x = 50 cos 40 = 38.3 m s^-1 and u_y = 50 sin 40 = 32.1 m s^-1.
Maximum height is reached when v_y = 0, at t = 32.1 / 9.81 = 3.28 s (the height there is 52.6 m, at a horizontal distance of 125.5 m).
The hillside is a straight line from the explosion at 20 degrees, so the rock lands on it when its height equals x tan 20: 32.1t - 4.905t^2 = (38.3 tan 20)t = 13.9t.
Solving, t = (32.1 - 13.9) / 4.905 = 3.71 s, which is later than 3.28 s.
Check: at 3.28 s the hillside beneath the rock is only 125.5 tan 20 = 45.7 m high, below the rock at 52.6 m, so the rock is still above the hill when it reaches its maximum height.

questions.question: A flare is launched to the right from a stationary boat at 30 degrees to the horizontal. Complete the diagram to show the path of the flare before it hits the sea.
questions.answer: A smooth parabola starting at the x on the boat, rising to the right at about 30 degrees to the horizontal, reaching a maximum height and then falling symmetrically to meet the sea to the right of the boat.
steps: Start the curve at the launch mark x, initially straight and sloping up to the right at 30 degrees to the horizontal (shallow, gradient tan 30 = 0.58).
Draw a smooth parabola: the horizontal velocity is constant and the vertical velocity decreases uniformly, so the curve flattens at a single maximum.
The descent should mirror the ascent (no air resistance), ending where the curve meets the sea surface, slightly beyond the symmetric point since the launch point is a little above the water.
The path must be a curve with no kinks, ending at the sea (not on the boat) to the right of the boat.

questions.question: A flare launched at 30 degrees to the horizontal reaches a maximum height of 42 m above the launch position. Show that it was launched at a speed of about 60 m s-1.
questions.answer: u = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 42) / sin 30 = 28.7 / 0.5 = 57 m s-1, which is about 60 m s-1 to 1 s.f.
steps: At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so u_y^2 = 2gh.
u = u_y / sin 30 = 28.7 / 0.5 = 57.4 m s-1, which is about 60 m s-1 to 1 s.f.

questions.question: The flare is visible from a maximum distance of 8 km. A rescue boat is 8.2 km from the distressed boat. The flare is launched towards the rescue boat at 30 degrees. Determine whether the flare travels far enough to be visible from the rescue boat.
questions.answer: Yes. The flare must travel at least 8.2 - 8.0 = 0.2 km towards the rescue boat, and its horizontal range is about 0.29 km (290 m), so it is visible.
steps: The flare must be within 8 km of the rescue boat, so it must travel at least 8.2 - 8.0 = 0.2 km (200 m) horizontally towards it.
Horizontal range R = u^2 sin 2 theta / g = 57.4^2 x sin 60 / 9.81 = 291 m (taking the landing level as the launch level).
291 m is more than 200 m, so the flare passes within 8 km of the rescue boat.
Even allowing for a launch point above the sea, the flare passes 200 m horizontally while still in flight, so the conclusion holds.

questions.question: State one assumption made in part (a)(iii).
questions.answer: Air resistance is negligible, so the flare follows a parabolic projectile path (alternatively: the flare lands at the same level as it was launched).
steps: The range calculation treats the flare as a projectile with only gravity acting.
So air resistance is assumed negligible.
The flare is also assumed to land at the same level as the launch point.

questions.question: A golfer hits a ball at 52 m s-1 at 41 degrees to the horizontal. Show that the vertical component of the initial velocity is about 30 m s-1.
questions.answer: Vertical component = 52 sin 41 = 34 m s^-1, which is about 30 m s^-1 to 1 s.f.
steps: The vertical component of the initial velocity is v_y = v sin theta, with v = 52 m s^-1 and theta = 41 degrees.
34.1 m s^-1 rounds to 30 m s^-1 to 1 significant figure, which agrees with 'about 30 m s^-1' (and 34.1 m s^-1 is used in later parts).

questions.question: The ground is 11 m higher than the starting point. Show that the time taken for the ball to reach the ground is about 7 s, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: Using u_y = 52 sin 41 = 34.1 m s-1, the ball lands at t = 6.6 s, which rounds to about 7 s.
steps: Take upwards as positive with u_y = 52 sin 41 = 34.1 m s-1 and displacement s = +11 m.
The larger root (the landing, after passing 11 m on the way up) is t = (34.1 + sqrt(34.1^2 - 4 x 4.905 x 11)) / 9.81 = 6.6 s.
6.6 s is about 7 s to 1 s.f.

questions.question: The hole is 250 m horizontally from the start. Deduce whether the ball landed within 5.0 m of the hole, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: No. The horizontal distance is 39.2 x 6.6 = 260 m, about 10 m beyond the hole, so it is outside 5.0 m.
steps: Horizontal component u_x = 52 cos 41 = 39.2 m s-1, constant without air resistance.
Time of flight to the ground (11 m higher) is 6.6 s.
Horizontal distance = 39.2 x 6.6 = 260 m.
260 m - 250 m = 10 m, which is more than 5.0 m, so the ball did not land within 5.0 m of the hole.

questions.question: A motorcyclist leaves a ramp at 25 degrees to the horizontal with speed 35 m s-1. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the initial velocity.
questions.answer: Horizontal = 35 cos 25 = 31.7 m s-1; vertical = 35 sin 25 = 14.8 m s-1.
steps: Horizontal component: u_x = 35 cos 25 = 31.7 m s-1.
Vertical component: u_y = 35 sin 25 = 14.8 m s-1.
The vertical component is upwards along the ramp direction.

questions.question: The end of the ramp is 3.0 m high and the river is 100 m wide. Deduce whether the rider lands on the other side, ignoring air resistance. Assume the far bank is at the same level as the base of the ramp.
questions.answer: Yes, marginally. The rider lands about 102 m horizontally from the ramp, which is past the 100 m width.
steps: Take upwards as positive: 3.0 m below launch gives s = -3.0 m, with u_y = 14.8 m s-1.
Horizontal distance x = 31.7 x 3.21 = 101.7 m.
101.7 m is greater than 100 m, so the rider clears the river and lands on the other side.

questions.question: Explain how air resistance would affect the jump.
questions.answer: Air resistance opposes motion, reducing the horizontal velocity and the vertical velocity, so the rider travels a shorter horizontal distance and may land in the river.
steps: Air resistance acts opposite to the velocity, so it has a horizontal component that reduces u_x over time.
A smaller horizontal velocity means less horizontal distance for the same flight time.
It also reduces the upward velocity, so the time in the air and the maximum height are both reduced.
The result is a shorter range, so the rider may fall short and land in the river.

questions.question: A ball leaves a bat at 37 m s-1 at 53 degrees to the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal distance travelled before it returns to the height it was hit from.
questions.answer: Horizontal distance = 37^2 sin 106 / 9.81 = 134 m.
steps: Time to return to launch height: T = 2u sin theta / g = 2 x 37 x sin 53 / 9.81 = 6.02 s.
Horizontal velocity u_x = 37 cos 53 = 22.3 m s-1, constant.
Horizontal distance = 22.3 x 6.02 = 134 m.

questions.question: A tennis ball machine projects balls horizontally from a height of 2.54 m. Show that the time to reach the ground is about 0.7 s.
questions.answer: t = sqrt(2h / g) = sqrt(2 x 2.54 / 9.81) = 0.72 s, about 0.7 s.
steps: Horizontal projection means the vertical initial velocity is zero.
h = 0.5gt^2 gives t = sqrt(2h / g).

questions.question: The ball lands on the ground 17.89 m from the machine. Calculate the velocity at which the ball is projected.
steps: The horizontal velocity is constant, so v = x / t.
This is the horizontal projection velocity, about 25 m s-1.

questions.question: Explain how increasing the initial horizontal velocity of the ball would affect the angle at which it hits the ground.
questions.answer: The fall time is unchanged, so the vertical velocity at impact is unchanged, while the horizontal velocity increases; the angle below the horizontal becomes smaller (the ball hits at a shallower angle).
steps: The vertical motion is independent of the horizontal motion, so the fall time stays at 0.72 s.
The vertical velocity at impact is v_y = gt = 9.81 x 0.72 = 7.06 m s-1, unchanged.
The horizontal velocity increases, so tan(angle) = v_y / v_x decreases.
The angle below the horizontal becomes smaller, so the ball hits the ground at a shallower angle.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at 500 m s-1 at 22 degrees to the horizontal from a site 2.0 km above sea level. A ship is 15 km horizontally away. Show that the projectile is vertically above the ship about 30 s after launch, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: t = 15000 / (500 cos 22) = 32.4 s, which is about 30 s to 1 s.f.
steps: Horizontal velocity u_x = 500 cos 22 = 463.6 m s-1, constant without air resistance.
The projectile is above the ship when its horizontal distance is 15 km: t = x / u_x.
t = 15000 / 463.6 = 32.4 s, which rounds to about 30 s to 1 s.f.

questions.question: Determine the height above sea level of the projectile as it passes over the ship, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: About 2930 m (2.9 km) above sea level: the projectile is 925 m above its launch point, which is 2.0 km high.
steps: Vertical component u_y = 500 sin 22 = 187.3 m s-1.
Height above sea level = 2000 m + 925 m = 2925 m.
Rounded, the projectile is about 2.9 km above sea level.

questions.question: Several projectiles are launched at the same speed at different angles. The horizontal distance first increases to a maximum and then decreases. Explain why the horizontal distance reaches a maximum, considering the components of the initial velocity.
questions.answer: The horizontal velocity (u cos theta) falls as the angle rises, while the time of flight (from u sin theta) rises; their product is largest at about 45 degrees.
steps: Horizontal distance = (u cos theta) x time of flight.
A larger angle gives a larger vertical component u sin theta, so a longer time in the air.
A larger angle also gives a smaller horizontal component u cos theta, so less horizontal distance per second.
At small angles the time is too short; at large angles the horizontal speed is too small. The maximum range occurs at about 45 degrees (slightly below it when landing lower than launch).

questions.question: A dart is thrown at 15.6 m s-1 at 5.0 degrees to the horizontal. Just before it hits the dartboard its vertical velocity is zero. Show that the time taken to reach the dartboard is about 0.14 s.
questions.answer: t = u sin 5.0 / g = 15.6 sin 5.0 / 9.81 = 0.139 s, which is about 0.14 s.
steps: Vertical component u_y = 15.6 sin 5.0 = 1.36 m s-1.
At impact v_y = 0, so v = u + at with a = -g gives t = u_y / g.

questions.question: Calculate the horizontal distance D travelled by the dart before it reaches the dartboard.
steps: Horizontal velocity u_x = 15.6 cos 5.0 = 15.5 m s-1, constant with no air resistance.
Time t = 0.139 s from part (a).

questions.question: A skier on a slope at 14 degrees to the horizontal has initial speed 7.1 m s-1 and moves 15 m down the slope. With resistive forces negligible, calculate the speed after 15 m.
steps: The component of weight along the slope is mg sin 14, giving acceleration a = g sin 14 = 2.37 m s-2.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as with u = 7.1 m s-1 and s = 15 m.

questions.question: A child throws a stone at 6.3 m s-1 at 55 degrees to the horizontal. Show that the vertical component is about 5 m s-1 and the horizontal component is about 4 m s-1.
questions.answer: Vertical = 6.3 sin 55 = 5.2 m s-1 (about 5 m s-1); horizontal = 6.3 cos 55 = 3.6 m s-1 (about 4 m s-1).
steps: Vertical component: u_y = 6.3 sin 55 = 5.16 m s-1.
Horizontal component: u_x = 6.3 cos 55 = 3.61 m s-1.
Rounded to 1 s.f., these are about 5 m s-1 and 4 m s-1.

questions.question: The stone leaves the child's hand 1.25 m above the water. Show that the greatest height above the water reached by the stone is about 3 m.
questions.answer: Max height above launch = 5.16^2 / (2 x 9.81) = 1.36 m; total = 1.25 + 1.36 = 2.6 m, which is about 3 m to 1 s.f.
steps: At the greatest height the vertical velocity is zero.
v^2 = u_y^2 - 2gh gives h = u_y^2 / (2g) = 5.16^2 / 19.62 = 1.36 m above the launch height.
Total height above water = 1.25 + 1.36 = 2.61 m.
This is about 3 m to 1 s.f.

questions.question: The inside of the tyre is 0.8 m in diameter and is 3.9 m from the side of the water. Deduce whether the stone lands inside the tyre.
questions.answer: Yes. The stone lands about 4.5 m from the edge, which is between 3.9 m and 4.7 m, so it lands inside the tyre.
steps: Components: u_x = 6.3 cos 55 = 3.61 m s^-1 and u_y = 6.3 sin 55 = 5.16 m s^-1 (upwards).
Taking up as positive, the stone ends 1.25 m below the launch point: -1.25 = 5.16t - 4.905t^2, so 4.905t^2 - 5.16t - 1.25 = 0 and t = 1.26 s (positive root).
Horizontal distance = u_x t = 3.61 x 1.26 = 4.5 m, measured from the point below the child's hand (the edge of the water).
The inside of the tyre runs from 3.9 m to 3.9 + 0.8 = 4.7 m from the edge, and 3.9 m < 4.5 m < 4.7 m, so the stone lands inside the tyre.
